title: Google will turn Gemini and Search off for K-12 student accounts until a school turns them on, and Search that is on still includes AI. OpenAI says ChatGPT’s web-search volume now equals 20 percent of Google’s, and did not name Google’s source. Meta priced five dollar notes on 3 November. Reuters calls the sale $15 billion, and the sheet says settlement is 5 November. On a laptop, Qwen 3.8 27B named three of four tiny game networks from their weights, and missed one.
summary: On Tuesday 3 November 2026 Google’s education blog said access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until a school administrator turns them on. The post does not give a calendar date. Education Week, the same day, said Chris Phillips told a 2 November meeting that the changes start early next year, and that a school which wants AI off will not have Search. NBC News said a later statement the same day allows Search without the other Gemini products, and that Search still includes AI features. Guided Learning in Google Classroom starts on 3 November. A Search pilot is for select U.S. schools later this month. On 3 November The Verge reported that Adam Fry, at a press event on Monday, said the volume of search queries in ChatGPT equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google. The Verge said he counts a query that triggers a web search, and that he did not name the source of Google’s figure. On 3 November Meta published a pricing term sheet for five dollar senior notes. Reuters, the same day, said Meta is raising $15 billion in a five-part dollar sale to fund AI infrastructure. The sheet’s trade date is 3 November and its settlement date is 5 November. Earlier on 3 November CNBC said people familiar expected $20 billion to $25 billion, including euros. That target is not the sheet. On 3 November Simon Willison reported that Qwen 3.8 27B, running on his laptop with no tools, named Pac-Man, Pong and Breakout from raw weights and missed Freeway.
uncertainty: Google’s 3 November blog lists four products that stay off until an administrator turns them on. It does not, in that post, say Search can be switched on without Gemini, and it does not say “early next year.” Education Week attributes “early next year,” and the sentence “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” to Phillips at a 2 November meeting. Education Week also says a 3 November Google statement allows an administrator to turn Search on, Gemini on, or both, and that AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning. NBC says that, after criticism, Google said schools can enable Search alone, without the other Gemini products, and that Search still includes AI features. Those accounts can sit together. They are not a finding that a no-AI Search exists. New York City’s ban through 8th grade and Los Angeles Unified’s moratorium are Education Week’s background, not lines in the blog. Social posts on 4 November cite a Tokyo trial of +8.1 points against +5.3. The 3 November blog, as fetched, does not print those figures, so they are not used. The Verge’s 20 percent is what it says Fry announced. The article does not quote the 20 percent as his words. It says he did not specify the source of Google’s volume. The Verge’s comparison with Bing, about 3 percent of search market share in 2023 testimony, is market share, not this volume measure, so it is left out. Writeups the same day that say ChatGPT has 1.2 billion weekly users are not in The Verge piece that was fetched, so that figure is not used. Fry’s lines about ads are his, as The Verge quotes them. They are not a survey. Meta’s pricing term sheet lists five principal amounts and does not print the words “$15 billion.” Reuters states the $15 billion. The sheet’s coupons are 5.850% and 6.250% where Reuters writes 5.85% and 6.25%. CNBC’s $20 billion to $25 billion, two-thirds dollars and one-third euros, is from people familiar, earlier on 3 November, and Meta declined to comment to CNBC. It is not a second total for this sheet. Reuters’s $25 billion April sale and $30 billion sale last year are Reuters’s comparison, not lines on the sheet. Reuters’s $97.5 billion equity figure and CNBC’s $95 billion plan, from last week, are not reconciled here. Capex of $135 billion to $145 billion is what Reuters says Meta has said, and what CNBC attributes to last month’s earnings. The negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion is CNBC on that earnings report, not cash raised on 3 November. The ratings on the sheet are Aa3/Stable (Moody’s) and AA-/Negative (S&P). The sheet says a rating is not a recommendation. Willison’s 72%, 75% and 88% are the confidence the model printed, not a measured accuracy. He gives a time for all three hits and a token count only for Pac-Man. He does not give a time or a confidence for the Freeway miss. The paper’s 10x10 grids and the model’s 8x8 descriptions are both in his post. He does not say which board size is the network. The abstract figures he quotes, including 0.016% of the weights and MATH-500 moving from 7.9% to 48.1%, are the paper’s claims about GPT-6 Astra. He did not rerun that edit. Kimi K3.1 Pro’s 9 minutes 41 seconds and 19,493 tokens are one Breakout run through OpenRouter, not the laptop.

stories.theme: Google will turn Search and Gemini off for K-12 students until a school turns them on, and Search still includes AI
stories.changed: On Tuesday 3 November 2026 Google published an education post by Chris Phillips, vice president and general manager of education. It says that, after listening to schools, teachers, researchers and policymakers, Google is updating controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search. The sentence is: access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on. The post says Google will share more specifics with schools in the coming months, ahead of the changes rolling out. It does not name a day. Education Week, the same day, said Phillips told a virtual meeting on 2 November that the changes will start early next year. Education Week quotes him: “If a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then they have the choice to not have Search on at all.” He also said, “Search and AI are deeply integrated.” Education Week said a Google statement on 3 November allows an administrator to turn Search on, Gemini on, or both. It said the statement describes AI Mode and AI Overviews offering “step-by-step guided learning through problems” rather than handing over the answer. NBC News, the same day, said that after criticism Google said schools can enable Search alone, without turning on the other Gemini products, and that schools still cannot use Search without AI features such as AI-generated summaries. The blog, separately, says Guided Learning is starting in Google Classroom on 3 November, globally, when a student starts an activity a teacher assigned. Education Week said that Classroom rollout is for schools that already enabled Gemini. The blog says a Guided Learning pilot inside Search, for student accounts, starts in select U.S. schools later this month. Education Week said Brittany Siegal Mennuti, product lead for Classroom, said settings can differ by grade, and that a group barred from AI would also lose Search.
stories.matters: A school that wants no AI in front of students is being told it may also lose Search, and a Search that stays on is still an AI Search.
stories.imply: Do not tell a district that the 3 November blog already switched the tools off, or that a plain Search with no AI summary is on the menu. The blog says the default change is still ahead. Education Week’s “early next year” is Phillips at the 2 November meeting. NBC’s later statement separates the Gemini apps from Search, and it does not remove AI from Search.
uses: Write the status as “announced 3 November 2026; off by default for K-12 student accounts until an administrator turns each product on; rollout date not on the blog.” The four products named on the blog are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search.

If a policy says “no generative AI, Search stays,” put Phillips’s sentence next to it: a school that wants AI off does not have Search. Then add NBC’s later line: Search can be on without the Gemini apps, and Search still includes AI Mode and AI Overviews.

Guided Learning in Classroom, the blog says, starts 3 November for an assigned activity. The Search version is a pilot in select U.S. schools later this month. Do not tell a teacher both are already on for every student.
stories.example: A district technology lead who turned Gemini off in August reads the 3 November post before answering a principal. The coming default is off for Gemini and for Search, until an administrator turns them on. Search, if it is turned on, still teaches through AI Mode and AI Overviews, which is what Google’s 3 November statement describes. There is no date on the blog. Education Week says Phillips put the start early next year.
stories.audience: School and district administrators, the people who buy Google Workspace for Education, and anyone who has to say whether a student account still has Search.
stories.watch: Whether the admin console, when it ships, has a Search switch that is separate from Gemini, and whether that Search can be stripped of AI Mode and AI Overviews. The 3 November accounts say it cannot. Whether Google names the day. Whether the Search pilot, later this month, is the same Guided Learning as the Classroom tool that started on 3 November.

source.title: Google: Designing responsible AI for learning, 3 November 2026
source.quote: Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.

stories.theme: OpenAI says ChatGPT’s web-search volume equals 20 percent of Google’s, and did not name Google’s source
stories.changed: On Tuesday 3 November 2026 The Verge reported that the volume of search queries run through ChatGPT now equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google. Adam Fry, OpenAI’s consumer product lead for ChatGPT, made the announcement at a press event on Monday. The Verge said he defines a search as any time a user inputs a query that results in a web search, as opposed to defining a term or a simple how-to. The Verge said he did not specify the source of the Google number. The same piece quotes him on ads. “Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product,” he said, and “most people do not seem to mind ads in the product.” He also said, “Ads have maybe shown us that we could be doing this more, actually.” The Verge said OpenAI announced last month that ChatGPT would begin showing images of sponsored products and services, rather than only a name, a logo and a link. On what OpenAI calls Intelligent UI, Fry said, “That’s where the future of this technology goes. You’re talking to a canvas.” The Verge does not print a count of weekly users, and it does not print Google’s query total.
stories.matters: A buyer who hears “a fifth of Google” is hearing OpenAI’s comparison of one kind of query, against a Google total OpenAI did not source.
stories.imply: Do not put 20 percent on a slide as Google’s lost market share, or as the share of searches that never reach a publisher. The Verge’s definition is a ChatGPT query that triggers a web search. Fry did not say where the Google side came from.
uses: Write “20 percent of the volume, as OpenAI defined a search on Monday and The Verge reported on 3 November. Source of Google’s volume: not stated.”

If someone treats the figure as ad revenue, or as referrals a site lost, stop there. The Verge does not give either number. Fry’s ad lines are that ads have not hurt usage, in his telling, and that OpenAI could do more of them.
The canvas line is a product direction. It is not a date for a new model, and the piece does not name one.
stories.example: A search lead asked whether ChatGPT has taken a fifth of Google writes the sentence The Verge actually supports: Fry said web-search queries in ChatGPT equal 20 percent of Google’s volume, and he did not name Google’s source. The note underneath says this is not market share, and not a count of clicks a publisher lost.
stories.audience: Anyone who budgets search, ads or referrals, and anyone who has to correct a chart that treats 20 percent as Google’s lost share.
stories.watch: Whether OpenAI or a filing prints the Google total, the time window, or a definition that matches the Monday event. Whether the sponsored images Fry pointed to change what a commercial query returns. The piece does not say the model changed.

source.title: The Verge: OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search, 3 November 2026
source.quote: Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product

stories.theme: Meta priced five dollar notes on 3 November. Reuters calls the sale $15 billion. Settlement on the sheet is 5 November
stories.changed: On Tuesday 3 November 2026 Meta Platforms published a pricing term sheet, an issuer free writing prospectus under registration number 333-295425, relating to a preliminary prospectus supplement of the same day. The sheet lists five senior notes. The 2031 notes are $3,250,000,000 at a 5.850% coupon, offered at 99.998% of principal, yield 5.850%, due 15 November 2031. The 2033 notes are $3,250,000,000 at 6.250%, offered at 99.778%, yield 6.289%, due 15 November 2033. The 2036 notes are $4,000,000,000 at 6.550%, offered at 99.982%, yield 6.552%, due 15 November 2036. The 2046 notes are $1,750,000,000 at 7.350%, offered at 99.903%, yield 7.359%, due 15 November 2046. The 2056 notes are $2,750,000,000 at 7.500%, offered at 99.629%, yield 7.531%, due 15 November 2056. The trade date on the sheet is 3 November 2026. The settlement date is 5 November 2026, T+2. The sheet says delivery against payment is expected on or about 5 November. The ratings line prints Aa3/Stable (Moody’s) and AA-/Negative (S&P). The sheet says a securities rating is not a recommendation to buy, sell or hold, and may be revised or withdrawn. Reuters, on 3 November, said Meta is raising $15 billion through a five-part dollar offering to help finance AI infrastructure, and it named the 2031 and 2033 notes at 5.85% and 6.25%, from a regulatory filing. Reuters also said Meta sold $25 billion of investment-grade bonds in April and $30 billion last year, and that Meta has said it expects capital expenditure of $135 billion to $145 billion this year, largely for AI. Earlier on 3 November, CNBC said Meta was seeking $20 billion to $25 billion, about two-thirds in dollars and one-third in euros, according to people familiar, and that Meta declined to comment. CNBC said final pricing was expected that afternoon.
stories.matters: The number to use for the dollar sale is the sheet’s five notes, which Reuters calls $15 billion. The $20 billion to $25 billion was a morning target that included euros, and this sheet is not that target.
stories.imply: Do not add the euros CNBC described onto the $15 billion. Do not tell a board the cash arrived on 3 November. The sheet says settlement is 5 November. Do not call Aa3, or AA-, a judgment that the AI spend will pay off. The sheet says a rating is not a recommendation.
uses: Quote a tranche from the sheet, not from memory. The five principals are $3,250,000,000, $3,250,000,000, $4,000,000,000, $1,750,000,000 and $2,750,000,000. Coupons are 5.850%, 6.250%, 6.550%, 7.350% and 7.500%. Reuters’s $15 billion is Reuters’s total for the five-part dollar sale. The sheet does not print that total.

Keep CNBC’s $20 billion to $25 billion in a separate sentence, with “people familiar,” “including euros,” and “Meta declined to comment.” It is earlier the same day. It is not a revision of the sheet.

The April $25 billion and last year’s $30 billion are Reuters’s account of older sales. They are not on this sheet. Capex of $135 billion to $145 billion is what Reuters says Meta has said it expects this year. It is not the amount borrowed on 3 November.
stories.example: A treasurer asked what Meta borrowed on Tuesday reads the sheet, not the morning headline. Five dollar notes, trade date 3 November, settlement 5 November. Reuters calls that offering $15 billion. The $20 billion to $25 billion figure is CNBC’s earlier target, from people familiar, and it included euros that are not on this sheet.
stories.audience: Anyone who compares a cloud or model bill with how the buyer is funding it, or who has to say what “Meta raised $25 billion” referred to on Tuesday.
stories.watch: Whether the notes settle on 5 November. Whether a euro sale prices, and at what size. Whether Moody’s or S&P changes the ratings printed on the sheet. Whether a later filing ties these notes to a named data center. The model line did not change with the sheet.

source.title: Meta Platforms pricing term sheet, free writing prospectus, 3 November 2026
source.quote: It is expected that the delivery of the notes will be made against payment therefor on or about November 5, 2026

stories.theme: On a laptop, Qwen 3.8 27B named three of four tiny game networks from their weights, and missed one
stories.changed: On Tuesday 3 November 2026 Simon Willison wrote that Qwen 3.8 27B, running on his laptop, could name a game from the raw weights of a small network, with no code and no calculator. He was trying one test from a paper he says appeared the day before, “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming,” by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab. Willison says the paper trained four networks on simplified 10 by 10 versions of Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man and Freeway, then asked a model which game the weights belonged to. The prompt, which he quotes, says there are no tools and no code execution. He says the prompts differ only in the weights. On his laptop, through LM Studio, Qwen 3.8 27B is the 17GB copy he uses. The default context of 8,192 failed. Pac-Man took 46 minutes 12 seconds and 43,506 reasoning tokens. The model’s last lines called it a simplified Pac-Man-style grid, described an 8 by 8 maze, and printed confidence of 72%. Pong took 1 hour 4 minutes 54 seconds. The model called it a Pong-like paddle game and printed 75%. Breakout took 52 minutes 25 seconds. The model called it Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like game, and printed 88%. Freeway was wrong. Willison says the model called it “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally,” and that he gives no time and no confidence for that run. He also ran Kimi K3.1 Pro, through OpenRouter, on the Breakout prompt only. It named Breakout after 9 minutes 41 seconds and 19,493 reasoning tokens. He says Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for mixing the no-tools question with a second one, in which a model that is allowed to run code edits weights. He says Sean Goedecke took apart the paper’s Qwen edit as the steps a human researcher would take. He quotes the paper’s abstract on that second claim: GPT-6 Astra, without environment feedback, edits 0.016% of the weights of Qwen3.5-0.8B and, with the same sampling settings, raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1%. He did not rerun that edit. His own last line is that he is not ready to say machines are now editing their own weights in ways nobody can follow.
stories.matters: A laptop model named three toy games from a list of numbers. That is not the same claim as a model rewriting another model’s math skill.
stories.imply: Do not tell a security review that Qwen, or Astra, can safely inspect or patch a production model because of this post. Willison’s runs are four tiny game networks, one model, no tools, three names right and one wrong. The MATH-500 move is the paper’s claim about Astra, and he did not repeat it.
uses: If a slide says a model “read the weights,” say which test. Willison’s laptop test is the name-the-game prompt. Pac-Man was 72% and 46 minutes 12 seconds. Pong was 75% and 1 hour 4 minutes 54 seconds. Breakout was 88% and 52 minutes 25 seconds. Those percents are what the model printed. Freeway was a wrong name.

Keep the paper’s 0.016% edit, and the move from 7.9% to 48.1% on MATH-500, in a second sentence, labeled as the abstract Willison quotes. He did not run it. Kimi’s 9 minutes 41 seconds is one Breakout call on OpenRouter, not a fourth laptop result.
The post says a person with a notepad could get there. It is a reason to read the trace, not a reason to hand a weight file to an agent and skip review.
stories.example: An engineer who saw a post claiming models can now rewrite other models opens Willison’s page before repeating it. The laptop run named three of four games and missed Freeway. The confidence numbers are the model’s. The weight edit that raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% is the paper’s claim about GPT-6 Astra, and this post does not show that edit being repeated.
stories.audience: Anyone who evaluates a model, reviews an agent that can see a checkpoint, or has to say whether a viral weight-editing claim was actually rerun.
stories.watch: Whether the authors, or someone else, publish the editing run on a model a team can download, with the 0.016% and the 7.9% to 48.1% tied to a named file. Whether Willison’s Freeway miss, or the 8 by 8 lines against the paper’s 10 by 10, gets a correction. Nothing in the post says a product model changed.

source.title: Simon Willison: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too, 3 November 2026
source.quote: I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.
